Neha Kharel

For someone who has ever held on to a memory tighter than reality, for someone who knows the sting of drifting apart from the person who once felt like home, and for someone who has loved in silence and lost without goodbye — this story is yours. Within these pages live Ishan and Anya, not just as characters, but as echoes of every friendship that was more than friendship, every love that remained unspoken, and every goodbye that came too soon. If you have ever felt the ache of what could have been, may you find yourself here.
Chapter 1
It was Sunday. I was tired from the week’s work. Just for a moment,
I picked up my phone to check messages— and that’s when my soul left my body.
It was a message from Rakshit, one of my friends from school. “Hey! Can we talk?”
His text usually used to be happy text. Even when he called, he would be bubbling with excitement.
But this time… it felt wrong.
I asked, “What’s wrong, Rakshit? Did something happen?”
He texted back too quickly, “Have you not heard about Anya?”
Anya? Her name alone did something to my chest, tightened it, twisted it.
I stared at the message, confused. Something felt off. I typed back, “What happened?”
The next message hit like a punch to the stomach. “She’s gone.”
Gone? Gone where? Gone from social media? Gone on a trip? Gone from the city? Gone from… me?
My brain scrambled for anything that made sense. But then, another message came.
“She jumped last night. Suicide.”
Everything stopped. The air thickened. My chest collapsed inward. I couldn’t move.
The walls, the fan, the phone in my hand—all blurred. A part of me wanted to laugh, like this was some cruel prank.
Anya? No. Not her. Not the girl who hummed while coloring the edges of her notebook. Not the one who feared thunder but danced in the rain. Not the girl who meant everything. Not Anya.
My fingers trembled as I re-read the message. “Jumped last night. Suicide.” Again. And again.
It didn’t feel real. The room was too quiet. Even the air seemed to hold its breath.
In the back of my mind, I still expected another message to come. “Sorry, wrong Anya.” “She’s fine. Just deactivated Insta or something.”
But no other message came. Only silence. And in that silence, my heart began to break.
I froze. “No… it can’t be true. No. This must be a joke. She can’t—she can’t do this to me.”
My flatmate had just returned. He saw me frozen, distressed, and asked what was wrong. I couldn’t answer.
I needed to see her house. Maybe someone was lying. Maybe it was a mistake. Maybe…if I got there fast enough—it wouldn’t be true.
I called her parents. Her father picked up. He didn’t speak. In the background, I heard crying. Wailing.
“Uncle—” He cut me off. “Just come home, son.” And hung up.
My flatmate stood in confusion. The silence. The crying. The way Uncle said those words, it all confirmed it.
I was about to lose consciousness, but my roommate caught me. He checked my phone. When he saw the messages, he hugged me tightly.
“This can’t be right. She can’t do this to me. Right? Max, please tell me this is a lie. Please.”
He helped me stand. He knew he had to take me there.
Her house wasn’t far. We used to live in the same neighborhood. A seven-minute walk. But that day, it felt like seven centuries.
Each step carried a memory.

The time she fell off her bicycle and I gave her a cartoon band-aid. The time she made me eat too many street-side pani puris. The time she cried outside tuition class because no one remembered her birthday—except me.
And now… she was gone. And I didn’t even know when she stopped being okay.
The house stood like an empty shell. Quietly grieving. Curtains drawn. A garland of white flowers hung above the door, the kind they put up for mourning.
I stopped. I couldn’t move. My chest hurt. I hadn’t seen her in months. I had been “busy.” Caught up in life.
I took a shaky breath and stepped inside.
When I twisted the doorknob, I saw her, her lifeless body on the ground.
Everything after that blurred. I didn’t hear anything. I don’t remember falling. I just remember her mother’s endless crying, her father trying to soothe her when he was more broken than anyone.
Her skin had turned pale… bluish. It was time for the final rites.
I felt like everything was ending. I remembered her smile. Her laugh. Her tears. The times she cried in my arms.
But this time, she didn’t. Why didn’t she come to me? I could have held her. Why did she choose this?
I bent down and touched her face. Cold. I hugged her, knowing this would be the last time.
I don’t know how much I cried. Usually, when I cried, she calmed me.
This time, she lay silently.
Didn’t she know? If she’s gone… she didn’t just leave.
She took my dreams. My comfort. My safe place. My happiness.
I saw my parents come in. Our families were close. The priest did his part. Her mother wasn’t conscious. Her father was barely standing. My father helped him.
Soon, they took her body for cremation. Tears flowed endlessly as we walked.
And when they lit the fire… it wasn’t just her body burning. It was my soul. The guilt. The fire of guilt. For not saving her.
When we came back, her house felt haunted. Quiet. And uncomfortable.
Chapter 2
When we reentered the house, I felt an
urgent need to see her room. I felt she was still there. My legs moved on their own, leading me upstairs. I didn’t ask for permission. I knew where her room was. I knew every step that led to it.
Her door was half open. I pushed it gently.
It hit me all at once.
The dreamcatcher still hung by her window, swaying slowly in the wind.
Her books were scattered across the floor, pages folded, some half-read.
Her favorite hoodie was thrown on the chair the one she wore every winter.
Her calendar still showed last month’s date. Everything was the same.
Except her.
She wasn’t there.
But her absence was louder than anything else. It screamed through the walls. It echoed through the things she left behind.
I walked to her desk. A notebook lay open, filled with doodles, half-finished poems, and lyrics. I ran my fingers across them.
Her handwriting hadn’t changed. Still small, neat, a little slanted.
I found a dried flower between two pages, pressed, forgotten, preserved.
And that’s when it broke me.
The tears came without warning. Hot, unstoppable, violent. My chest heaved as I fell to the ground, knees hitting the wooden floor. I held onto her chair like it could anchor me, but it didn’t.
I sobbed. Like a child.
Like someone who’d lost not just a friend, but time,
chances, forgiveness.
I kept whispering her name, over and over again, as if that would bring her back.
Anya. Anya. Anya…
But she didn’t answer.
I don’t know how long I stayed on the floor. It could’ve been five minutes or five hours. Grief doesn’t keep time, it just fills space. It sits on your chest and doesn’t let you breathe properly.
When I finally lifted my head, the room felt different. Still hers, still silent, but now watching me. Like it knew I didn’t belong here anymore.
I looked around slowly.
Her bookshelf was covered in dust. I walked to it, trailing my finger over the spines of novels we once talked about, books we promised we’d read together but never did.
The Fault in Our Stars Kafka on the Shore
The Perks of Being a Wallflower
Each one bruised my memory. Her voice echoed faintly in my head.
“You never read the endings,” she once teased me. “Endings are scary,” I had said.
And maybe that’s why I hadn’t seen hers coming.
On the corner of the table sat a candle—until. Next to it, her Polaroid camera. I picked it up. There was still film inside. I pressed the button. One photo clicked out.
Just black. No flash. I had forgotten how to use it. I sat down on her bed.
It was neatly made, too neatly. Like someone had smoothed the sheets for the last time. The pillow smelled like jasmine shampoo. I closed my eyes and breathed it in.
And then something caught my eye.
Just above her pillow, taped gently to the wall, was a piece of paper.
A note.
Not the note. Not a suicide note.
But something else. Something older.
It was folded, worn, maybe even forgotten. I pulled it off gently and opened it.
It wasn’t addressed to anyone. Just a short paragraph in her handwriting; blue ink, the kind that fades with time.

“I hope when someone finds this, they remember the girl I used to be. Not the version that faded quietly. Remember the one who laughed too loudly, sang too off-key, and dreamed too much. I just want someone to say I mattered. Even if only for a moment.”
My breath caught.
My hands shook again.
And just like that, another tear slipped down my face.
She had been leaving pieces of herself everywhere.
Like she knew she was disappearing slowly and wanted to be remembered in fragments.
I looked around the room again. Suddenly, everything felt like a message.
Her messy handwriting on the whiteboard: “Don’t forget to be gentle with yourself.”
The stack of post-it notes on the mirror, filled with half-written affirmations.
The playlist open on her laptop titled “when my mind is too loud.”
I opened the laptop’s lid, but it was dead. Charger missing. Of course.
Then I noticed the box. It was under the bed.
Barely visible, hidden like a secret.
A small wooden box, painted with stars, flowers, clouds. I remembered this box.
We made it together during a summer camp. She painted stars. I painted the moon.
“I’ll put my favorite memories in here,” she had told me. “I’ll put snacks,” I had replied, and she had laughed so hard she nearly cried.
I pulled it out gently.
It was surprisingly light.
Inside, there were photos. Of us. From when we were kids. Laughing in the schoolyard. Dressed as trees in a school play. Holding melting ice creams with chocolate smeared on our chins.
I ran my fingers over the photos.
And then beneath them, I found a crumpled receipt. A café we used to visit every Thursday after school. And scribbled on the back:
“I sat alone this time. The coffee didn’t taste the same.”
I felt sick.
All this time, she had been reaching out. Not with calls or texts, but through silence, through tiny acts of remembering. She had been waiting for someone to notice. For me to notice.
And I hadn’t.
I placed everything back into the box.
My body felt heavier now, like every memory was a stone in my chest.
Outside, the sky had begun to cry.
Raindrops tapped on the window, soft at first, then louder. The wind howled like it missed her too. The dreamcatcher spun slowly, helplessly.
I lay down on her bed.
It still held her warmth, her absence, her quiet goodbye.
And for the first time in years, I closed my eyes and let myself fall apart.
No pretending. No running.
Just grief, raw and echoing through my bones.
And beneath it, a single question that would not stop burning:
Why didn’t I notice?
The rain outside had grown louder.
Each drop hit the glass like it was trying to say something I couldn’t understand.

I didn’t know how long I had been lying there, on her bed, in her scent, in the hollow of her absence. Grief doesn’t knock politely. It enters and breaks every lock, every breath, every muscle holding your heart together.
Somewhere downstairs, a door creaked. A cough.
Murmured voices.
But in this room, there was only silence. And questions.
Why didn’t she call me?
Why didn’t she scream louder? Why didn’t I ask if she was okay?
Maybe I had been too busy. Maybe I thought she’d always be there. Maybe we all think that, that people don’t break unless we hear the sound of them cracking.
But not all pain is loud. Some people drown quietly.
I sat up slowly. My hands were still trembling.
The box still lay beside me, her memories carefully tucked inside.
But something in me needed more.
I didn’t know what I was looking for. Maybe closure.
Maybe one more reason to believe this wasn’t real. Or maybe I was hoping I’d find something that would tell me this wasn’t my fault.
I turned to her closet. It creaked open.
The same vanilla and jasmine scent slipped out, familiar and ghostly.
Clothes still hung there, ironed and clean.

I touched one of her scarves. I remembered her wearing it the winter we skipped school and got caught in a hailstorm. She had wrapped it around both of us like a promise we never made but always understood.
I remembered the time she used to cry, saying she didn’t have any clothes while we went out.
I opened the drawers slowly. A jewelry box.
A broken watch.
A few folded wrappers from chocolates she couldn’t resist.
Then the bottom drawer jammed.
I ignored it, thinking it hadn’t been used for a long time.
I left her room and went downstairs.
I saw aunty was not eating. I knelt down.
“Aunty, you know something?” She looked at me. I took her hand.
“Anya once told me something. She said she once had a fever, and you were so worried you didn’t eat. Is that right?”
She nodded.

“And you know, the time she came crying to me and told me she never liked that you skipped food for her or anyone. She said she just wanted you to live for yourself. And today, do you think she would be happy that you are skipping food?”
She looked at me and said,

“And did she think we would be happy if she did this to us? She thinks we can live for ourselves when we know we failed as parents for her. How does she even expect that? You know, son, even if she is my daughter, I will never forgive her. We thought she was our support system, but not only did she prove us wrong, she gave us the worst pain of our lives.”
I don’t even know when tears started to fall from my eyes.
I hugged her.
“Aunty, please don’t do this to yourself. Please eat, aunty. Please, for me. I couldn’t save her, but I don’t want to lose you too, aunty.”
I knew she loved me as her son.
I took a plate and fed her. She ate a little.
“Aunty, now take your medicine and try to sleep, okay? I will come tomorrow.”
She was not letting me leave, but uncle took her to bed.
My parents insisted I stay, but I left for my flat with my flatmate.
While heading out, I saw Rakshit. When he saw me, he hugged me.
“Rakshit, where did she jump from?” Rakshit looked at me and said,
“Ishan, We will talk about this later. Today, you go and rest.”
I nodded and left for my flat.
CHAPTER 3
Then we reached the flat, I took out a bottle of drink, the only thing
that could numb my pain, besides her. My flatmate Max joined me. I was on my third glass when he asked,
“Hey, it’s not really appropriate to ask, but can you tell me about her? I mean, how did you two meet, and what happened?”
I hadn’t planned to say anything that night. But maybe pain chooses its own timing.
“You ever watch a flower die slowly?”
Max didn’t answer. He just looked at me, the kind of look that said, No, but I think I’m about to.
“It’s not dramatic. Not loud. It doesn’t scream.
One day it’s there, colorful, open, full of life. The next day, it leans. Quietly.
Like it just gave up on being beautiful.”
I exhaled, hands on the floor behind me, leaning against the wall of our shared apartment.
It was past midnight.
Max’s guitar leaned forgotten in the corner. The window was slightly open, and the streetlight spilled orange onto the floor between us.
“That’s how she faded,” I said. I met Anya on a Tuesday.
I remember because it was raining, and my socks were soaked by the time I entered class 1B.
I was the new kid, shy, awkward, and not very good at smiling on cue.
The teacher made me stand in front of thirty strangers and say my name.
My voice cracked halfway through. They laughed.
Except one.
A girl in the second row with ink-stained fingers, crooked ponytails, and shoes two sizes too big.
She didn’t laugh.
She tilted her head and smiled.
That was it.
The first time anyone ever looked at me like I was something more than background noise.
Later that day, at lunch, she walked up to me and held out her hand.
“Strawberry eraser for your boring grey one?” I blinked at her.
“Why?”
“Because yours looks sad.” I took hers. She took mine.
And just like that, she took me, too.
From that day on, we were inseparable. She was fire; I was water.
She was loud; I was calm.
She danced in puddles; I avoided mud. But somehow, we made sense.
She’d drag me into trouble, and I’d pull her out just in time.
We built treehouses in her backyard. Held funerals for broken toys.
Had a secret handshake that changed every month.
She was my first sleepover, my first birthday party, my first “you’re my person.”
And maybe, just maybe, my first love. Though I didn’t know it yet.
By class 5, we had “our bench” in the school garden.
By class 6, we’d started writing letters, even though we saw each other daily.
Stupid ones. Like:
“Dear Anya, today I kicked a rock and it hit a teacher. Should I run away and become a monk?”
She’d reply:
“Dear Monk Ishu, bring me along. I want to pet the goats.”
We were kids.
But everything felt… forever.
I called her Anya the Brave because she once climbed the tallest slide without blinking. And she called me Ishu.
We promised we’d never grow up. But of course, we did.
By class 8, Anya stopped coming to school.

There was a girl who used to bully Anya a lot. She never told me she was being bullied. It was Rakshit who told me that Anya had been bullied at school. He also told me she didn’t want to tell me because the bully was the girl I used to like.
I felt so many emotions at that time.
I felt anger at that girl, but guilt and helplessness at myself, that my best friend was suffering and she didn’t tell me, and I was too dumb to find out by myself.
One day, when she came out of her dance class, I saw bruises on her knee.
Maybe she noticed me looking at them because she avoided me for a while.
She ran away to somewhere else.
I followed her for some time and found her sitting on the bench where we used to gossip.
“Anya!” I ran toward her and sat beside her.
“Anya! Why are you doing this? Why are you hiding these things from me?”
She tried to deny it.
“Look, it’s not a big deal, okay? And these bruises are from—”
“Anya, tell me who did it.” She was still trying to deny it.
“Ishan, please, it’s my problem. Don’t get into it.” I was shocked by her words.
“Anya, since when is there a ‘yours’ or ‘mine’ in our friendship? Are you even hearing yourself? If you’re
still not telling me, then I don’t think I’m your friend anymore—”
I couldn’t even finish my sentence before she hugged me tightly and started sobbing on my shoulder.
I caressed her hair.
She may be Anya the Brave, but she was just a baby girl to me.
“Anya, it’s okay. I’m here for you.”
After some time, I said, “Anya, tell me who did it now.”
She wiped her tears and whispered the name: “Aisha.”
I knew it.
It could be her, which is why she wasn’t telling me. “What is she telling you, Anya?”
My breath caught. A sudden wave of nausea hit me. I couldn’t believe what I was hearing.
“She… what?” I asked, my voice barely above a whisper.
Anya still wasn’t looking at me. Her eyes were fixed on the ground, her fingers tangled together, knuckles pale.
“She said if I told anyone, especially you, she’d ruin me,” she murmured. “She’d destroy everything. My dignity, my life, my name. She even said she knew how to make it look like I wanted it.”
I felt something inside me break. Like a string snapping. Like a fire lighting up every inch of my body.
“Why didn’t you tell me sooner, Anya?” My voice cracked. I wanted to scream, to cry, to hug her and break things at the same time. “I would’ve—”
“I was scared, Ishu,” she whispered. “I didn’t want to become a ‘story.’ I didn’t want you to hate me or look at me differently. And you… you liked her. I thought you’d choose her.”
My eyes widened. “Anya… no. Never. I liked her because I didn’t know her. But you? I loved you, because I knew you. Every part of you.”
She looked at me then. Her eyes were glassy, shimmering with the pain she had buried for so long.

“I felt dirty, Ishan. Every time she smirked at me in the hallway… every time she walked past like she owned my silence….I felt like I was disappearing. And I hated that I was too weak to fight back.”
“You weren’t weak,” I said, my voice shaking. “You were scared. And alone. And no one...no one should have to go through that.”
I reached out and took her hands in mine.
“I’m here now. And I swear to you, Anya… I won’t let her get away with this.”
She leaned into me, her body trembling. I wrapped my arms around her, feeling how fragile she’d become, like glass, like one wrong word would shatter her completely.
She had fought so much, all on her own. And I had been so blind.
That night, as we sat on that old bench, the sky above us silent and still, I realized something.
She didn’t need a savior. She just needed someone to notice.
And from that moment on, I vowed I would never stop noticing her again.
Chapter 4
That night, something shifted between us.

The silence that used to be comfortable now felt sacred, like it was holding every unsaid word, every wound we couldn’t voice yet. We sat on that bench till the stars came out, saying nothing. Just breathing in each
other’s presence.
After that day, I never let her walk alone.

I started waiting outside her classes, pretending I just “happened to be there.” I’d offer to walk her home, buy her chocolate when her smile looked tired, and slip little notes into her textbooks when she wasn’t looking.
She never said much about Aisha again.
But the fear lingered in her eyes, especially when she saw Aisha in the hallway.
I never confronted Aisha directly. Anya begged me not to. She said she just wanted peace, not drama. And I respected that. But I made sure Aisha knew I knew.
My eyes followed her like shadows. I stopped smiling around her. And she stopped smiling back.
By the time we reached Class 10, Anya had built herself up again, quietly, brick by brick. Her laugh was softer, her walls higher, but her courage? Still there.

She joined the drama club, not because she loved acting, but because it made her feel seen. I watched her from the back row during her first performance, nails digging into my palm as she delivered her lines with trembling bravery.
She didn’t know I cried that night. No one did.
But I did, because I was proud. Because she had survived. Because she was still trying, even after all the world had taken from her.
And I was scared. Scared of how close I had come to losing her before I even knew she was fading.
In high school, Anya and I became something more than best friends—but we never named it.
Maybe we were afraid that giving it a name would change it. That calling it "love" might break the spell. So, we kept it hidden, safe, unspoken, and ours.
We started doing everything together.

Morning walks before school, shared bus rides, reading the same book and fighting over which character was better. On Saturdays, we had a ritual, she’d bring cold coffee, I’d bring chips, and we’d lie under the tree near the abandoned library, talking about everything and nothing.
She once told me her biggest dream was to become a writer.
“Not a famous one,” she said, smiling up at the sky. “Just someone whose words feel like home to someone else.”
I laughed. “Then start writing, Wordsworth.”
“Shut up,” she giggled, tossing a chip at me. “I’ll write only if you promise to be the first person to read every word.”
“I promise,” I said, not realizing how much that promise would mean one day.
She kept a tiny red diary, never let it leave her bag. Said it was for “moments that matter.” She’d sometimes read me little things from it. A line. A poem. A memory.
Like the time we got caught in the rain, and I gave her my hoodie.
Or the time she failed a math test and I brought her candy and a handmade “Math Hates You Too” certificate.
“Why do you keep writing about me so much?” I asked once, half-joking.
She looked at me, eyes soft.
“Because you’re the only part of my life that doesn’t feel heavy.”
I didn’t know what to say to that. So, I just smiled and squeezed her hand. We never talked about it again, but it stayed with me.
Everything stayed.
By Class 11, we had become a team.
If someone messed with her, they dealt with me. And if someone teased me, she’d turn into a hurricane. Once, a senior made fun of my stammer during a debate. I was too humiliated to respond.
Anya? She stood up in the middle of the hall, pointed straight at him, and shouted:
“At least he’s brave enough to speak.” The whole hall went quiet.
So did I.
I looked at her like I was seeing her for the first time all over again.
Anya was still healing, still scarred, but she had built her strength in silence. She didn’t need saving anymore. She was saving me now.
Then came the time she wrote a play for the school fest.
A raw, emotional story about a girl who hides her sadness behind laughter.
Everyone clapped. Teachers called it “mature,” “impressive.”
I saw the truth in every word.
I walked up to her after the show, heart pounding, and whispered, “Was that about you?”
She shrugged. “Maybe a little.”
That night, I wanted to tell her everything.
That I knew she still carried pain. That I loved the way she kept trying.
That I was terrified of losing her again.
But instead, I just held her hand while we walked home.
And she didn’t let go.
The months that followed were the golden hours of our story.
We didn't need confessions to understand what we meant to each other. I think sometimes love doesn't need words, it lives in the spaces between them.

There was a winter trip organized by the school. Everyone else was excited about snowball fights and selfies. Anya and I sneaked out early one morning before the others woke up. The world was painted white, the trees bowed with snow, and our breaths curled like smoke in the cold air.
She stood in the middle of the road, arms wide, head tilted back, eyes closed.
“You know what this moment feels like?” she whispered.
“What?”
“Like time is holding its breath.”
And so was I, because all I could look at was her.
She turned to me, snowflakes in her hair, and smiled that crooked smile that could bring me to my knees.
I didn’t say anything. Just memorized it.
Every blink. Every second.
Because deep down, I had a strange ache, like all of this was too perfect to last.
And maybe I was right.
It started with a phone call she didn’t answer. Then two.
Then a weekend when she didn't show up for our usual Saturday spot under the tree.
I thought maybe she was sick. Or tired.
Or maybe school was stressing her out.
I waited for her message. But it never came.
When I saw her next at school, her smile was smaller.
Forced.
Her eyes were puffy like she hadn’t slept. I asked her if everything was okay. She nodded too quickly.
“I’m fine, Ishu. Just a little headache. Exams, you know?”
But I knew her. Better than anyone. This wasn’t exams.
This was something deeper.
Something heavier.
I started noticing the changes, how she stopped writing in her red diary. How she began flinching when her phone buzzed. How her laughter became rarer, thinner, like it was scared of being real.
I didn’t push her. Maybe I should have.
Maybe I should have grabbed her shoulders and said, “Tell me. I can handle it. I want to handle it.”
But I didn’t.
Because I trusted her silence the way I had trusted her voice.
Until the silence started pushing me away.
One evening, I saw her walking home alone. I ran to catch up. She looked startled.
“Ishu! You scared me.”
“Why didn’t you tell me you left school early?” “I wasn’t feeling well,” she mumbled.
Then, before I could say more, her phone rang. She looked at the caller ID and silenced it.
Twice.
I noticed her hand shake. “Who’s that?” I asked gently.
She shrugged. “Just… family stuff.” “Everything okay?”
She paused. A second too long.
Then forced a smile. “Yeah. Just messy. I’ll handle it.”
“You can talk to me, you know.”
“I know, Ishu,” she said, almost too sharply. And then, softer, “I know. I just… need time.” I nodded.
But inside, I was screaming.
Because I felt her slipping through my fingers.
And I didn’t know how to hold on without hurting her.
A week later, Rakshit told me something that made my chest cave in.
“Her dad’s business is going bankrupt.” “What?”
“Yeah. She didn’t tell you?”
“No.”

And then, her voice. Not out loud, but in my head. Every word was her voice, the way she spoke when she was trying not to cry.
The first few lines hit like a soft wind. Then the next like a knife.
And then the rest… like a storm I couldn’t breathe in.

I read about the bullying, things she never told me. My chest tightened so hard it hurt to inhale. I read about her parents, and I remembered the nights she’d text me “I’m tired” and disappear. I read about the birthday. God, the birthday.

I had waited for hours that day, my phone glued to my palm. I’d told myself she was busy, she’d come later. I’d even saved a seat for her at the café. I sat there like an idiot, guarding it from strangers.
She never came. And now I knew why.
And it broke me in a way that felt final.
By the time I reached the part where she said she loved me too much to let me drown with her… I couldn’t see the paper anymore. My tears had blurred her words into water stains.
I pressed the letter to my face. It still smelled faintly of her, the same faint vanilla and rain she always carried.
It wasn’t enough. It wasn’t her.

I curled forward, my forehead touching the floor, the letter crumpled in my grip. My chest was heaving, but no sound came out at first. Just this silent, shaking grief that felt like it was tearing muscle from bone.
Then the sobs broke through. Loud, desperate, ugly. The kind of sound you make when you’ve lost something you’ll never get back.
Her words kept replaying in my head. Name your daughter Anya.
How the hell was I supposed to even think about having a daughter, when I couldn’t even survive this moment?
I wanted to scream at her. I wanted to hold her.
I wanted to tell her she was wrong, that I would have carried her storm, her weight, all of it. That I wouldn’t have drowned. That I would have kept her afloat even if it killed me.
But the truth was…
She wasn’t here to listen anymore.
The room felt too small, the air too thick. I stumbled to my desk, where the old paper boat sat — the one we made years ago. I picked it up, my tears
falling onto its edges, making the paper soft, fragile, like her.
And I broke again.
That night, I slept on the floor, clutching the letter and the paper boat like they were the last pieces of her I had left.
Because in some cruel way, they were.
And in the quiet, with my eyes burning and my heart refusing to slow down, I whispered into the darkness,
"I’ll always be your Ishu. Even if you’re not here to call me that anymore."
Morning.
I woke to sunlight sneaking through the half-drawn curtains. For a second, I forgot. For a second, I thought I’d hear her voice telling me to get up.
But the silence was absolute. And it hit me all over again.
The letter was still clutched in my fist, wrinkled from the night. My body ached from the floor, but I couldn’t bring myself to move. Not yet.
When I finally did, my eyes landed on something near the side of her bed, a small wooden box.
I pulled it toward me slowly, like it might shatter if I touched it wrong. I lifted the lid.
Inside was her life in pieces.
The bracelet I gave her in grade 6, faded but still whole.
The paper boat we made that rainy day, its edges soft from age but still holding its shape.
The candy wrapper I folded into a heart. She had kept it.
Old letters I’d written her silly notes from class, birthday wishes, random thoughts. Every single one was there, folded neatly, as if she’d been guarding them.
My throat tightened so much I could barely breathe.

Underneath it all, I found something else , my old hoodie. The one I gave her years ago when she was shivering at the bus stop. I thought she’d forgotten about it. She hadn’t. It still smelled faintly of her shampoo, and I pressed it to my face, my tears soaking into the fabric.
And then… at the very bottom… a photograph.
It was us. Sitting by the lake, the sunlight in her hair. She wasn’t looking at the camera, she was laughing at something I said. I wasn’t looking at the camera either. I was looking at her.
I pressed the photo to my chest, my whole body shaking.

I don’t know how long I sat there. Minutes. Hours. Time stopped meaning anything. I just kept tracing her handwriting on the folded notes, touching the things she touched, as if they could bridge the impossible gap between us.
At some point, her mother knocked softly and left a glass of water by the door. She didn’t say anything. She didn’t need to.
When I finally stood, I didn’t put the box back. I hugged it to my chest like it was her. Like if I let go, she’d vanish completely.
I walked to her window and looked outside, the same view she must have seen a thousand times. The street, the sky, the world that had gone on without her.
And I whispered into the still air,
"I’m still your Ishu. Always. Even if you’re not here to call me that anymore."
Chapter 16
I don’t know how long I’d been sitting there, staring at the same

patch of floor, the world around me nothing more than a blur of silence. My fingers were numb, my eyes dry and sore from the hours, maybe days, of crying. Then my gaze landed on the edge of her photo frame, peeking out from under a stack of papers on the table. I
reached for it without thinking.
It was the photo from that trip years ago, the one where she had that stubborn little smile,

the one that told you she knew life wasn’t easy but she’d stand against it anyway. I traced the curve of her cheek with my thumb, almost expecting the warmth of her skin to seep through. But it was just cold glass.
And then it hit me, the weight of it, she would never take another photo. That smile was now frozen in time, and all the dreams she carried… they were stranded too, unless someone picked them up.
For the first time since she left, I felt something different. Not less pain, no, the pain was still there, sharp and deep, but a flicker of… purpose.
I remembered the nights we stayed up talking about the book we’d write. How she said words

could outlive people, how she wanted to publish something that mattered. I remembered the tiny dreams she’d collect like seashells, learning to bake a perfect cake, watching the sunrise from a mountaintop, holding her own book in her hands.
All of it felt unfinished. And if I stopped here, if I let myself fade with her, then it would all stay unfinished.
“No,” I murmured, voice breaking. “No, I’m not letting it end like this.”
I didn’t even realize I was speaking to her photo until I saw my own reflection in the glass, red-eyed and hollow but… alive.
“I’ll finish the book, Anya. I’ll chase every dream you didn’t get to. And one day, when it’s out there in the world, I’ll know you’re somewhere, smiling at me like you did that day.”

The tears came again, but this time they weren’t only from loss, they were from the terrifying, fragile knowledge that I had something to live for. I kept holding her photo for a long time, afraid that if I set it down, that flicker of purpose might disappear. My hands felt heavy, but my chest… lighter, in a strange way. I ran my thumb over the edge of the frame once more before placing it carefully on my desk, right beside the open notebook that had been gathering dust for months.

The pen lay where I had abandoned it last, a single unfinished sentence staring back at me, mocking me with its incompleteness. For weeks, maybe longer, I hadn’t been able to write. Every time I tried, the words felt hollow, meaningless.
But now… now the silence felt different.

I pulled the chair closer and sat down. My hands shook as I picked up the pen, not from fear this time, but from the weight of knowing this mattered. The story wasn’t just mine anymore. It was hers. Ours.

The first line I wrote was clumsy, but I didn’t stop to fix it. I wrote another, and another. The pen scratched against the paper, the ink bleeding into the page like it had been waiting all this time.

Somewhere in the back of my mind, I could hear her voice, teasing, encouraging, sometimes laughing at my awful metaphors. I could almost imagine her leaning over my shoulder, reading the words as I wrote them.
And for the first time in forever, I didn’t feel like I was writing into an empty world.
I was writing to her.
I knew it wouldn’t be easy, chasing down all those dreams, bringing them to life, but I had made a promise. And I wasn’t going to break it. Not to her. Not to myself.
When I finally put the pen down, I realized hours had passed. The pages were filled. My tea had gone cold. And her photo was still watching over me from the corner of the desk, her smile unchanged.
Only now, I felt like I understood it.

That night, I didn’t fall asleep right away. I just sat there, my head resting on folded arms, staring at her photo until my eyes blurred. The ache was still there, deep and unshakable, but now it lived beside something else, something warmer.
It was strange… the pain didn’t vanish, but it no longer felt like it was pulling me under. It felt like a reminder, a sharp edge keeping me awake, alive, pushing me forward.
Somewhere between the grief and the promise I’d made, I realized this was not an ending. Not for her, and not for me.
Maybe my life had been shattered, but now I had the pieces. And piece by piece, I would build something she would be proud of.
I whispered one last time into the quiet room, “For you, Anya.”
And in the stillness, I almost believed I heard her whisper back.
Chapter 17
Time, I realized, doesn’t heal everything. It changes us. It carries

sorrow into the quiet corners of our days and teaches us how to live with it. But I never forgot her, never a single day. Anya was with me in the ink of every page I wrote, in every whispered hope, in the smallest of decisions. She had shaped the man I had
become.

Holding the book in my hands, I felt her there, not as a ghost, but as the quiet, persistent fire that had
always guided me.

Life moved forward, slowly, carefully. Love returned to me, softly, unexpectedly. I married, and the day our daughter was born, I stared down at her tiny, delicate face, her fingers curling around mine, and the world felt infinite and fragile all at once. Watching her grow brought a flood of memories, her laughter echoing through our home, her small triumphs and stumbles, the spark of curiosity in her eyes. Each time she smiled, I felt the Anya I had loved all over again, her courage and joy flowing into the next generation. I remembered her insistence on capturing every small moment, her love for tiny victories and quiet sunsets. And I realized that this was the ultimate fulfillment of her dream: to be remembered not just in stories, but in life itself.

And my writing… our writing… it became more than words on paper. I published the book we had begun together, dedicating it to her. I included lines she had once whispered to me, her favorite metaphors, her secret jokes hidden between sentences. Every review, every message from someone touched by the words reminded me that she was still shaping the world, even after she had
gone. I named my successes after her, every small achievement a tribute to the girl who had shown me how to keep dreaming.

In quiet moments, when the house was still and my daughter slept, I would look at her photo on my desk, the same one I had held on that fateful night, and whisper, “This is for you, Anya. For every dream you carried, for every story we shared, for every life you still touch.”

And in that silence, I felt it: peace. Not the absence of sorrow, but the presence of love, memory, and purpose. Anya had never truly left me. She had become a part of everything I was, everything I did, and everything I would ever be.

She lived in my words, in my family, in the life I had built. I saw her in the first steps of my daughter, in the pages of our book that reached strangers across the world, in every sunrise I watched with a quiet smile. And finally, after all the grief, all the sleepless nights, all the empty mornings, I understood. The best way to honor her wasn’t to hold onto the past, it was to live the life she had inspired me to live, fully, fearlessly, and with every ounce of love I had left to give.
And so I lived, for her, through her, and with her in every heartbeat.
Epilogue
Even now, I find myself searching for her in the smallest places.
A breeze that feels too familiar.
A song that sounds like something she would hum under her breath.

The quiet way the night holds me when I’m alone. She isn’t here, yet she is everywhere. I used to believe tomorrow was just another day, a blank space waiting to be filled. But now I know tomorrow carries her. Not her face, not her voice, but the weight of her absence, the echo of her laughter, the warmth of her memory.

I thought I lost her the day she left this world, but the truth is, I carry her in every decision, every word, every fragile hope I allow myself to hold. She is not gone; she has simply changed her place. She lives in my grief, in my pages, in my quiet victories.
Anya exists in my every tomorrow. Not as a shadow of what was, but as a promise of what will always be.
And now, I step in, not as Ishan, not as Anya, but as the one who wrote them into being.

To you, Ishan: your voice has carried this story, but your silence carried the weight. You searched for her in the world and found her in yourself. You loved her in ways you could never say, and now your life is proof that love does not end with loss. It bends, reshapes, but never ends.

To you, Anya: though paper holds your voice and ink holds your pain, you are more than the sadness that closed your story. You are laughter that still lingers, bravery that was misunderstood, love that will outlast even these words. You exist in him, in me, and now in everyone who turned these pages.

And to you, the reader: this was never just a story. It was a memory disguised as fiction, a wound disguised as words. “You exist in my every tomorrow” is not only for Anya—it is for everyone we have loved and lost, everyone whose absence reshaped us.
If you’ve reached this last page and felt her presence, even for a moment, then she has lived again. And maybe that’s enough.
She exists. In Ishan. In me. And now,
in you.
